label: Approaching, not achieved
rationale: Every 2025 estimate published in 26H1 is a new record: GCB fossil CO2 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.0%), IEA energy CO2 38,082 MtCO2 (+0.4%) and Carbon Monitor fossil+industry CO2 37.2 GtCO2 (+0.7%); only GCB total CO2 dipped slightly, due to lower land-use emissions as El Niño ended. Growth has slowed to a plateau (global fossil power generation fell 0.2%, China and India flat), but China's CO2 rose 2% in Q1 2026 and the IEA expects the shock-driven 2026 oil-demand fall to rebound above the 2025 level in 2027, so the peak is not definitively behind us. Caveat: the milestone covers all greenhouse gases, but no global 2025 total-GHG estimate was published within 26H1, so CO2 estimates serve as the proxy.

label: Worsening
rationale: The Mauna Loa CO2 concentration hit new records in 26H1: a 432.34 ppm monthly mean in May 2026 (+1.83 ppm on May 2025) and a 433.95 ppm daily mean on 1 May. The 10-year trend (NOAA Jan->Dec, 2016-2025) is 2.56 ppm/yr at MLO (2.53 global); its dip from 2.64 is mechanical (El Niño year 2015 left the window) and half-decade means still rose (2.51 -> 2.61 ppm/yr), so there is no structural slowdown. Year-on-year growth temporarily slowed (+1.48 to +2.26 ppm in Jan-Jun 2026), matching in direction the Met Office forecast of a slower 2026 annual-mean rise that it attributes to La Niña-like conditions, but it remains far above the 1.33-1.79 ppm/yr that IPCC 1.5°C pathways require.

label: Approaching, not yet achieved
rationale: Global fossil CO2 emissions still rose to a record 38.1 GtCO2 in 2025 (+1.1%), so the peak has not been reached. China (32% of global emissions) has been flat or falling for 18 months, driven by clean energy, which may mark the beginning of the end.

label: Distant — 53 GtCO2e/year to eliminate
rationale: Global GHG emissions were 53.2 GtCO2e in 2024 and fossil CO2 hit a record in 2025, far from net zero. Net-zero targets cover 77% of global GDP, but 2025 was a year of retreat (US Paris withdrawal, banks exiting NZBA, delayed corporate targets) and most IEA net-zero pathway benchmarks are off track.

label: Under pressure
rationale: 2024 was the first calendar year to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial (WMO 1.55°C), though the long-term Paris metric remains ~1.3-1.4°C. WMO gives 70% odds the 2025-2029 average also exceeds 1.5°C, and the 1.5°C carbon budget is virtually exhausted.

label: ⚠️ Accelerating in the wrong direction
rationale: Atmospheric CO2 reached 426.5 ppm (Nov 2025) with the annual peak exceeding 430 ppm for the first time, and the 2023-2024 increase of +3.5 ppm was the largest on record. The jump was driven by continued fossil emissions, El Niño-weakened land sinks and record wildfires.

label: Distant — ~54 GtCO2e/year to eliminate
rationale: EDGAR 2026 put total greenhouse-gas emissions excluding LULUCF at 54.1 GtCO2e in 2025, up 0.7% on 2024, and GCB 2025 put total CO2 (fossil + land-use change) at a preliminary 42.2 GtCO2 in 2025, so net emissions remain nowhere near zero. At the 23 September 2026 UN Climate Summit, Guterres said emissions are still rising and a temporary 1.5°C overshoot is expected, calling for national fossil-fuel transition roadmaps, of which Germany's (23 September) is only the third after France and the Netherlands, while the US President attacked the IMO Net-Zero Framework for shipping ahead of its December 2026 adoption vote. Corporate commitments keep growing (700+ Climate Pledge signatories targeting net zero by 2040) but do not change the global picture.

label: Plateau, peak not confirmed
rationale: The total-GHG gap is now filled: EDGAR 2026 put greenhouse-gas emissions excluding LULUCF at 54.1 GtCO2e in 2025, up 0.7% on 2024, alongside record 2025 fossil CO2 (GCB 38.1 GtCO2, +1.0%; IEA energy CO2 38,082 MtCO2, +0.4%). For 2026, Climate TRACE estimates total GHG for January-July 0.3% above the same period of 2025, while Carbon Brief projects global fossil CO2 to fall about 0.5% in 2026, a decline driven by the Strait of Hormuz oil shock that the IEA expects to reverse in 2027 when oil demand rises above its 2025 level. China's CO2 remains below its 2023-24 peak (Q2 2026 -1%, H1 up marginally) but India's CO2 rose 3.7% in H1 2026, so the peak is still not definitively behind us.

label: Under growing pressure
rationale: Berkeley Earth (24 September 2026) put August 2026 at 1.71 ± 0.11°C above 1850-1900, the warmest August on record, and judged the 2026 annual mean 'all but certain' to exceed 1.5°C (likely 1.536-1.642°C) with a 93% chance of a record year, as a record-strength El Niño (daily Niño 3.4 anomaly 3.11°C on 21 September) is expected to add further warming in 2027. These are single-month and single-year anomalies; the latest long-term (Paris-metric) warming estimate in the ledger is WMO's ~1.3-1.4°C for 2024, so the 2°C ceiling has not been breached. However, the GCB puts the remaining 50% 1.5°C budget at 170 GtCO2 from 2026 (about 4 years at 2025 emissions) and emissions have not yet peaked, so holding peak warming below 2°C remains plausible but increasingly strained.

label: Worsening, El Niño spike ahead
rationale: After the record 432.34 ppm May 2026 monthly mean, NOAA Mauna Loa (MLO) monthly means fell seasonally to 429.13 ppm in July and 427.55 ppm in August 2026, still 1.26 and 2.07 ppm above the same months of 2025, so the concentration keeps rising and the July gain was only a continuation of the temporary 26H1 slowdown. The 10-year trend (NOAA Jan->Dec growth, 2016-2025) is unchanged at 2.56 ppm/yr at MLO (2.53 global), far above the 1.33-1.79 ppm/yr 2020s decadal average that the Met Office says IPCC 1.5°C scenarios require. New since July, Zeke Hausfather (28 September 2026) expects an El Niño-driven spike in the atmospheric CO2 growth rate in 2027, similar to the record 3.33 ppm MLO growth of 2024, as models put the 2026-27 El Niño's Niño 3.4 peak around 4.1°C; this is a qualitative projection, but it points to re-acceleration rather than relief, so the status stays red.

label: Regressing: 427.35 ppm (2025); 10-yr growth 2.56 vs 2.15 ppm/yr, need <=1.79 (tier 1)
rationale: The assessed quantity, the 10-year mean of NOAA Mauna Loa Jan->Dec CO2 growth, rose to 2.56 ppm/yr for 2016-2025 from 2.15 ppm/yr for the previous non-overlapping window 2006-2015 (+0.41, about 1.9 standard errors), and half-decade means rose monotonically (1.97, 2.34, 2.51, 2.61 ppm/yr), so the growth rate is moving away from the goal of <= 0. The tier-1 benchmark, a 2020s mean growth of at most 1.79 ppm/yr for IPCC C1 1.5°C pathways (Met Office), is far exceeded (2.61 ppm/yr for 2021-2025). The Jan-Jun 2026 year-on-year slowdown (+1.48 to +2.26 ppm) spans less than a window and has a named reversing cause (La Niña-like conditions), so it is discounted as a transient; the record 2025 annual mean of 427.35 ppm is reported, not scored.

label: Distant: net CO2 42.2 Gt (2025), ~53 GtCO2e GHG (2024), not yet falling; ETA >10 yrs
rationale: Net emissions are not yet declining: GCB puts total CO2 (fossil + land-use change) at 42.4 GtCO2 in 2024 and a preliminary 42.2 GtCO2 in 2025, with fossil CO2 at a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.0%), and total-CO2 growth only slowed to 0.3%/yr over 2015-2024. Extrapolating that trend gives no evidenced path to approximately zero within 10 years (the emissions peak itself is not yet behind us), so the ETA is over 10 years and the status is red. Net-zero targets covering 77% of global GDP are pledges, which cannot lift the status, while US Paris withdrawal (legacy record) is a policy obstacle rather than the determining block.

rationale: Not achieved: every 2025 estimate is a new record (GCB fossil CO2 38.1 GtCO2, +1.0%; IEA energy CO2 38,082 MtCO2, +0.4%; Carbon Monitor 37.2 GtCO2, +0.7%), so no verified achievement event exists. There is measurable progress on the milestone's own quantity: total CO2 growth slowed from 1.9%/yr (2005-2014) to 0.3%/yr (2015-2024), global fossil power generation fell 0.2% in 2025 and China and India plateaued, which extrapolates to a peak within a few years. But China's CO2 rose 2% in Q1 2026 and the IEA expects oil demand to rebound above its 2025 level in 2027, so a peak that is 'definitively' behind us (confirmed by sustained decline) has a credible ETA of 5-10 years, hence yellow.

label: Distant: ~1.3-1.4°C long-term warming, still rising; peak needs net zero, ETA >10 yrs
rationale: Peak warming can only be established, and held below 2°C, once warming stops rising, which requires global net CO2 emissions near zero; those emissions were still at a record in 2025 (fossil CO2 38.1 GtCO2) and have not peaked, so there is no evidenced path to a warming peak within 10 years. Long-term warming is about 1.3-1.4°C (WMO, legacy record) with 2024 at 1.55°C, and the remaining 50% 1.5°C budget of 170 GtCO2 (about 4 years of 2025 emissions) shows how fast budgets are being used. The 2°C ceiling is not breached, but distance to the goal is reported, not scored; on the ETA rule the status is red.
